messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 46
  gender: Non-binary
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Software Engineer
  trauma_type: Police violence
  pcl5: 54

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Feeling Happy: Feeling happy or relaxed, Conflict: Confrontations, Others Cycling: People cycling
  Threat: Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
  Memory: No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it
  Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you, Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Arjun Mehta is a 46-year-old non-binary software engineer who presented for an initial psychological assessment approximately eight months after an incident of police violence that left them profoundly altered in ways they struggle to articulate even to themselves. Married for eleven years and generally regarded by colleagues as steady and methodical, Arjun arrived at the intake session visibly scanning the waiting room before selecting the chair furthest from the door and closest to the corner wall — a choice, they explained quietly, that had become automatic wherever they went.

The incident occurred on a Saturday afternoon in late spring. Arjun had been cycling home from a farmers' market, unhurried, carrying a cloth bag of produce, when they were stopped by two officers responding to a description that bore only the loosest resemblance to them. What followed escalated with a speed that Arjun still cannot organise into a coherent sequence. There was a command, then a second command overlapping the first, then physical contact — hands on their shoulders, then the ground, then weight. The specifics blur and fragment even as Arjun attempts to reconstruct them. They recall the texture of the pavement against their cheek and the sound of a radio crackling nearby, but the connective tissue between these sensory fragments remains missing. When asked in session to walk through what happened, Arjun repeatedly stops mid-sentence, not from reluctance alone but because the story genuinely does not cohere for them — the before and after exist, but the middle collapses into sensation without narrative.

In the weeks following the incident, Arjun noticed that the sight of someone cycling past on the street would produce an abrupt tightening in the chest, a flooding of dread so complete and physical that they would need to stop walking and grip a nearby surface. They have not ridden their own bicycle since. Their commute, once a point of quiet pride, is now navigated entirely by car with specific routes chosen to minimise the likelihood of passing the intersection where it happened. At work, Arjun sits with their back to the wall in every meeting room and positions their monitor so that the office entrance remains visible in their peripheral field. They have begun arriving before colleagues and leaving after most have gone, finding the open-plan floor difficult to tolerate when it is populated. Their manager noted a drop in participation in team standups, attributing it to stress; Arjun has said nothing to correct this interpretation, in part because they are convinced that something about them — some visible mark of what occurred — is already apparent to anyone who looks carefully enough. They have come to feel that their distress is written on their face, that colleagues who glance at them in the corridor are registering something shameful and broken.

Any confrontation, however minor — a disagreement in a code review, a terse email from a stakeholder — now carries a charge entirely disproportionate to its content. Arjun's body responds as though the stakes are existential, and they have begun avoiding any professional situation that might involve pushback or friction, declining to raise concerns they would previously have voiced without hesitation. Their spouse has observed that Arjun flinches at raised voices on television and has stopped laughing easily, as though happiness itself has become unsafe. Arjun confirmed this with some difficulty: moments of relaxation or pleasure have begun to feel precarious, as though ease is a condition they no longer have the right to occupy or one that will be interrupted without warning.

What frightens Arjun most, beneath the specific fears, is the collapse of a framework they had quietly relied upon their entire adult life — the sense that the world operated according to legible rules, that harm came with warning signs one could read and respond to. That framework is gone. They are certain now that danger can arrive from any direction and that knowing someone's role or intention offers no real protection. What finally brought them to seek help was their spouse's observation, offered gently one evening, that Arjun had stopped being present in their shared life. Arjun is not sure they can recover what was lost, but they have come hoping, at minimum, to understand why they no longer feel like themselves.
